content.title: About
content.content: Bread, oatmeal, toasted is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of a slice of whole‑grain bread soaked with cooked oatmeal and lightly toasted to a golden crust. It combines the crunchy texture of bread with the soft, nutritious body of oatmeal, providing a balanced breakfast or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination boosts fiber and slowly digestible carbohydrates.
Toasting enhances the nutty aroma typical of whole‑grain bread.
Traditionally prepared in Scandinavian countries as a quick breakfast for hunters and fishermen.
Oatmeal helps stabilize blood sugar levels after meals.
Conveniently packaged in single‑serve portions for school lunches.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber from whole grain bread and oatmeal supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans from oatmeal help lower cholesterol and support the immune system.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide steady energy without rapid glucose spikes.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, supporting blood and bone health.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some versions may contain added sugar; choose unsweetened options if monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because it combines bread and oatmeal, it can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to wheat or oats should avoid this product.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the package. Enjoy it as a snack, add to yogurt, use in sandwiches, or cut into cubes for salads. For extra crunch, briefly warm in a toaster.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in the original packaging or an airtight container. For longer shelf life, keep refrigerated to prevent mold growth. Check the expiration date on the package.

carrots-canned-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Carrots, canned, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Canned carrots are cooked carrot pieces packed in glass or metal jars without added fat. The product retains most of the nutrients of fresh carrots and is convenient for long‑term storage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned carrots are often used as an ingredient in soups, stews, and salads.
During canning carrots are usually blanched, which helps preserve their bright orange color.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
A sealed jar can keep canned carrots good for 2‑3 years.
In the US and Canada canned carrots are classified as a ready‑to‑eat vegetable.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in carrots is converted to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in carrots promotes regular bowel movements and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes this product suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt for preservation; people monitoring sodium intake should take this into account.

items.title: Carrot allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Bacterial contamination if packaging is compromised
items.content: Damaged or bulging cans can harbor pathogenic bacteria; such products should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned carrots can be eaten cold in salads, added to hot soups and stews, used in pie fillings, or served as a side dish with meat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer carrots to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 5‑7 days.

ice-cream-sundae-hot-fudge-topping.title: Ice Cream Sundae with Hot Fudge

content.title: About
content.content: Ice cream sundae with hot fudge is a classic dessert consisting of vanilla ice cream scoops drenched in a warm, thick chocolate fudge sauce, often topped with whipped cream, a cherry, and nuts. The sauce is made from dark chocolate, butter, sugar, and cream, giving it a rich, sweet‑bitter flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first sundae appeared in the United States in the early 1920s as a way to serve ice cream in a glass with a topping.
The term “fudge” comes from the English word for a soft caramel‑like confection.
Hot fudge is served immediately after preparation to maintain the contrast between the warm sauce and cold ice cream.
Traditional recipes often include pecans or walnuts for added crunch.
There are many sauce variations, including salted caramel, sea‑salt, or spice‑infused versions such as cinnamon.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Ice cream, as a dairy product, provides calcium essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: The milk ingredients supply a modest amount of protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The sugary dessert rapidly replenishes glucose stores, which can be useful after intense physical activity.

items.title: Antioxidants in chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate in the fudge is rich in flavonoids that may benefit cardiovascular health.

items.title: Psychological boost
items.content: Enjoying a favorite treat can increase serotonin levels, improving mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of diabetes when consumed frequently.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Ice cream contains lactose, so those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: If nuts are added, they may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The fudge and whipped cream make the dessert very calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Temperature shock
items.content: The hot sauce can cause mouth burns if served too hot.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sundae in a large glass or bowl, drizzle hot fudge over the ice cream, add whipped cream, a cherry, and sprinkle with nuts. Eat with a spoon, allowing the sauce to soften slightly for the perfect temperature contrast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ice cream in the freezer at –18 °C in an airtight container. Hot fudge is best prepared just before serving; any leftover sauce can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 3 days and reheated gently over low heat.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickles NFS are classic brined cucumbers seasoned with dill, garlic, and spices. They have a crisp texture, refreshing sour taste, and a subtle aromatic note. The product is made from fresh cucumbers grown in environmentally friendly conditions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Russian pickling methods date back over 200 years.
Cucumbers are often blanched in cold water before brining to preserve crunchiness.
Vinegar in the brine helps retain vitamin C and other nutrients.
Mustard seeds are commonly added to the brine for a characteristic flavor.
Pickles are a popular ingredient in salads, sandwiches, and appetizers.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A medium pickled cucumber contains about 15 kcal, making it an excellent choice for diet plans.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Fermentation creates beneficial bacteria that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Cucumbers provide vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: With over 90% water content, pickles help maintain fluid balance.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt may be unsuitable for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to dill or garlic
items.content: Some people may react to the spices used in the brine.

items.title: Bacterial growth if stored improperly
items.content: Storing pickles above 4 °C for prolonged periods can allow pathogenic bacteria to develop.

items.title: Added sugar in sweet‑sour varieties
items.content: Some recipes contain added sugar, increasing the calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickles can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, burgers, or used in cold soups such as okroshka.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pickles in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in their original brine. Once opened, consume within 2‑3 weeks. Discard if mold appears or the smell changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato, scalloped, ready-to-heat, with meat (code 4215) is a dish made of thinly sliced potatoes baked in a creamy sauce with selected meat. It is supplied in a sealed package that can be heated in a microwave or oven.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scalloped potatoes are a traditional dish in Europe and North America.
Cream and cheese are often added to the sauce for a rich flavor.
The meat may be beef, pork, or a blend of both.
The product can be stored in the freezer for up to 12 months.
Heating usually takes 5‑7 minutes in a microwave or 15‑20 minutes in an oven.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide slowly digestible energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in potatoes supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Meat‑derived protein
items.content: The meat adds complete protein needed for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins present
items.content: Vitamins B6 and B12 from the meat participate in metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The dish may contain a relatively high amount of salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The sauce often includes cream and cheese, which can trigger reactions in those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Heat safety
items.content: When reheating, ensure the interior reaches at least 75 °C to eliminate possible bacteria.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Because of cream and meat, the scalloped potatoes can be calorie‑dense; moderation is advised for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the package in a microwave (500 W for about 5‑7 minutes) or in an oven (180 °C for 15‑20 minutes). Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs or grated cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours and do not store in the refrigerator for more than 48 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Ranch dip is a creamy sauce made from mayonnaise, sour cream, and a blend of herbs and spices, delivering the classic dill, garlic, and onion flavor. It is intended for serving with vegetables, chips, crackers, and other snacks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ranch is one of the most popular sauces in the United States, with consumption exceeding 1.5 billion servings per year.
The sauce was originally created in the 1950s at the Hidden Valley Ranch restaurant in California.
Its signature taste comes from a mix of dried herbs (dill, parsley), garlic powder, and onion powder.
Ranch dip is often used in culinary experiments: as a marinade, salad dressing, and even in baked goods.
In Russia the product is sold as "Ranch dip, regular" in a 422‑gram package.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The sour cream and dairy components provide calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamin A
items.content: Contains vitamin A, which supports vision and immune function.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Dairy ingredients may contribute to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The sauce contains milk and can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Ranch dip is calorie‑dense and rich in fats, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The salt level may be a concern for people monitoring sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dip with fresh vegetables, potato wedges, chicken nuggets, crackers, or use it as a dressing for salads and sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep Ranch dip refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in its original container. After opening, use within 7‑10 days. Do not freeze.
